claim: The COP9-Signalosome (CSN) regulates cullin–RING ubiquitin ligase (CRL) activity and assembly by cleaving Nedd8 from cullins.
source: The COP9-Signalosome (CSN) regulates cullin–RING ubiquitin ligase (CRL) activity and assembly by cleaving Nedd8 from cullins.
evidence: This is a well-established function of CSN supported by the literature and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Free CSN is autoinhibited.
source: Free CSN is autoinhibited, and it remains unclear how it becomes activated.
evidence: Supported by structural data showing E104 of Csn5 occupying the active site zinc in free CSN.

claim: Both CSN and neddylated substrate undergo large conformational changes upon binding.
source: Both CSN and neddylated substrate undergo large conformational changes upon binding, with important roles played by the N-terminal domains of Csn2 and Csn4 and the RING domain of Rbx1 in enabling formation of a high affinity, fully active complex.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structural analysis and comparison with crystal structures.

claim: The N-terminal domains of Csn2 and Csn4 play important roles in enabling formation of a high affinity, fully active complex.
source: Both CSN and neddylated substrate undergo large conformational changes upon binding, with important roles played by the N-terminal domains of Csn2 and Csn4 and the RING domain of Rbx1 in enabling formation of a high affinity, fully active complex.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis studies showing deletion of these domains affects binding affinity and catalytic activity.

claim: The RING domain of Rbx1 plays an important role in enabling formation of a high affinity, fully active complex.
source: Both CSN and neddylated substrate undergo large conformational changes upon binding, with important roles played by the N-terminal domains of Csn2 and Csn4 and the RING domain of Rbx1 in enabling formation of a high affinity, fully active complex.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis studies showing deletion of the RING domain dramatically reduces catalytic activity.

claim: The RING domain is crucial for deneddylation.
source: The RING domain is crucial for deneddylation, and works in part through conformational changes involving insert-2 of Csn6.
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis showing ~18,000-fold reduction in kcat when RING is deleted.

claim: The RING domain works in part through conformational changes involving insert-2 of Csn6.
source: The RING domain is crucial for deneddylation, and works in part through conformational changes involving insert-2 of Csn6.
evidence: Supported by suppression analysis showing Csn6-ΔINS2 partially rescues the defect of ΔRING substrate.

claim: Nedd8 deconjugation and re-engagement of the active site zinc by the autoinhibitory Csn5 glutamate-104 diminish affinity for Cul1/Rbx1 by ~100-fold.
source: Nedd8 deconjugation and re-engagement of the active site zinc by the autoinhibitory Csn5 glutamate-104 diminish affinity for Cul1/Rbx1 by ~100-fold, resulting in its rapid ejection from the active site.
evidence: Supported by binding affinity measurements comparing substrate and product binding to different CSN mutants.

claim: The ~100-fold reduction in affinity results in rapid ejection of Cul1/Rbx1 from the active site.
source: Nedd8 deconjugation and re-engagement of the active site zinc by the autoinhibitory Csn5 glutamate-104 diminish affinity for Cul1/Rbx1 by ~100-fold, resulting in its rapid ejection from the active site.
evidence: Supported by koff measurements showing rapid dissociation of product from wild-type CSN.

claim: These mechanisms enable a dynamic deneddylation-disassembly cycle that promotes rapid remodeling of the cellular CRL network.
source: Together, these mechanisms enable a dynamic deneddylation-disassembly cycle that promotes rapid remodeling of the cellular CRL network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic parameters measured and their implications for cellular dynamics.

claim: Cullin–RING ubiquitin ligases comprise one of the largest families of regulatory enzymes in eukaryotic cells.
source: Cullin–RING ubiquitin ligases comprise one of the largest families of regulatory enzymes in eukaryotic cells (Deshaies and Joazeiro, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: There are as many as 240 different CRL enzyme complexes.
source: With as many as 240 different enzyme complexes, these E3s control a broad array of biological processes (Skaar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: CRLs control a broad array of biological processes.
source: With as many as 240 different enzyme complexes, these E3s control a broad array of biological processes (Skaar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: CRLs comprise seven distinct cullin–RING cores.
source: CRLs comprise seven distinct cullin–RING cores, each of which interacts with its own dedicated set of adaptor–substrate receptor complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRL architecture.

claim: Each cullin-RING core interacts with its own dedicated set of adaptor–substrate receptor complexes.
source: CRLs comprise seven distinct cullin–RING cores, each of which interacts with its own dedicated set of adaptor–substrate receptor complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRL architecture.

claim: A key mechanism that controls the activity of all known CRLs is the conjugation of the ubiquitin-like protein Nedd8 to a conserved lysine residue in the cullin subunit.
source: A key mechanism that controls the activity of all known CRLs is the conjugation of the ubiquitin-like protein Nedd8 to a conserved lysine residue in the cullin subunit (e.g. K720 in human Cul1)(Enchev et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: K720 is the conserved lysine residue for neddylation in human Cul1.
source: A key mechanism that controls the activity of all known CRLs is the conjugation of the ubiquitin-like protein Nedd8 to a conserved lysine residue in the cullin subunit (e.g. K720 in human Cul1)(Enchev et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a specific factual detail about Cul1 structure.

claim: Nedd8 conjugation stabilizes a profound conformational change in the C-terminal domain of the cullin.
source: The available structural and biochemical data indicate that Nedd8 conjugation (neddylation) stabilizes a profound conformational change in the C-terminal domain of the cullin.
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Neddylation loosens the interaction of the WHB domain with the RING subunit.
source: It loosens the interaction of the WHB domain with the RING subunit, allowing both of them to sample a greater conformational space (Duda et al., 2008), thereby enhancing the ability of the RING domain to promote ubiquitin transfer to substrate (Duda et al., 2008; Saha and Deshaies, 2008; Yamoah et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Neddylation allows the WHB domain and RING subunit to sample a greater conformational space.
source: It loosens the interaction of the WHB domain with the RING subunit, allowing both of them to sample a greater conformational space (Duda et al., 2008), thereby enhancing the ability of the RING domain to promote ubiquitin transfer to substrate (Duda et al., 2008; Saha and Deshaies, 2008; Yamoah et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published structural studies.

claim: Neddylation enhances the ability of the RING domain to promote ubiquitin transfer to substrate.
source: It loosens the interaction of the WHB domain with the RING subunit, allowing both of them to sample a greater conformational space (Duda et al., 2008), thereby enhancing the ability of the RING domain to promote ubiquitin transfer to substrate (Duda et al., 2008; Saha and Deshaies, 2008; Yamoah et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published biochemical studies.

claim: Nedd8 protects Skp1/Cul1/F-box (SCF) complexes from the substrate receptor exchange factor (SREF) Cand1.
source: In addition to direct effects on ubiquitin ligase activity, Nedd8 also protects Skp1/Cul1/F-box (SCF) complexes from the substrate receptor exchange factor (SREF) Cand1 (Pierce et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2013; Zemla et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Cand1 binds unmodified SCF complexes and promotes rapid dissociation of the F-box protein (FBP)/Skp1 substrate receptor–adaptor module from the Cul1/Rbx1 core.
source: Cand1 binds unmodified SCF complexes and promotes rapid dissociation of the F-box protein (FBP)/Skp1 substrate receptor–adaptor module from the Cul1/Rbx1 core.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of Cand1 function.

claim: Cand1 can be dissociated from Cul1 by a different FBP/Skp1 complex.
source: Cand1 can subsequently be dissociated from Cul1 by a different FBP/Skp1 complex, and as a result Cand1 functions as an SREF that accelerates the rate at which Cul1/Rbx1 comes to equilibrium with different FBP/Skp1 substrate receptor–adaptor complexes (Pierce et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: Cand1 functions as an SREF that accelerates the rate at which Cul1/Rbx1 comes to equilibrium with different FBP/Skp1 substrate receptor–adaptor complexes.
source: Cand1 can subsequently be dissociated from Cul1 by a different FBP/Skp1 complex, and as a result Cand1 functions as an SREF that accelerates the rate at which Cul1/Rbx1 comes to equilibrium with different FBP/Skp1 substrate receptor–adaptor complexes (Pierce et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: The SREF activity of Cand1 is tightly restricted by Nedd8.
source: Importantly, the SREF activity of Cand1 is tightly restricted by Nedd8.
evidence: Supported by subsequent statements and citations.

claim: Cand1 is not able to bind stably to Cul1 and promote dissociation of FBP/Skp1 when Cul1 is conjugated to Nedd8.
source: Cand1 is not able to bind stably to Cul1 and promote dissociation of FBP/Skp1 when Cul1 is conjugated to Nedd8 (Liu et al., 2002; Pierce et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: The rate of Nedd8 deconjugation serves as the gateway for the exchange cycle.
source: Of particular significance is the rate of Nedd8 deconjugation, because it serves as the gateway for the exchange cycle; once Nedd8 is removed, a CRL complex is susceptible to the potent SREF activity of Cand1, and its substrate receptor can be exchanged (Pierce et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the established roles of Nedd8 and Cand1.

claim: Once Nedd8 is removed, a CRL complex is susceptible to the potent SREF activity of Cand1.
source: Of particular significance is the rate of Nedd8 deconjugation, because it serves as the gateway for the exchange cycle; once Nedd8 is removed, a CRL complex is susceptible to the potent SREF activity of Cand1, and its substrate receptor can be exchanged (Pierce et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: Deconjugation of Nedd8 is mediated by the COP9-signalosome (CSN).
source: Deconjugation of Nedd8 is mediated by the COP9-signalosome (CSN), which is an eight-subunit Nedd8 isopeptidase (Lyapina et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: CSN is an eight-subunit Nedd8 isopeptidase.
source: Deconjugation of Nedd8 is mediated by the COP9-signalosome (CSN), which is an eight-subunit Nedd8 isopeptidase (Lyapina et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: The enzymatic activity of CSN resides in its Csn5 subunit.
source: The enzymatic activity of CSN resides in its Csn5 subunit, which contains a metalloprotease active site referred to as the 'JAMM' domain (Cope et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: Csn5 contains a metalloprotease active site referred to as the 'JAMM' domain.
source: The enzymatic activity of CSN resides in its Csn5 subunit, which contains a metalloprotease active site referred to as the 'JAMM' domain (Cope et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: The JAMM domain has the general structure E76-Xn-H138-X-H140-X10-D151.
source: The JAMM domain has the general structure E76-Xn-H138-X-H140-X10-D151 (the subscripts refer to the sequence position of these residues in human Csn5), wherein the H and D residues coordinate a zinc ion.
evidence: This describes the structural features of the JAMM domain.

claim: In the JAMM domain, the H and D residues coordinate a zinc ion.
source: The JAMM domain has the general structure E76-Xn-H138-X-H140-X10-D151 (the subscripts refer to the sequence position of these residues in human Csn5), wherein the H and D residues coordinate a zinc ion.
evidence: This describes the catalytic mechanism of the JAMM domain.

claim: The fourth zinc-coordination site in the JAMM domain is occupied by a water molecule that also forms a hydrogen bond to E76.
source: The fourth zinc-coordination site is occupied by a water molecule that that also forms a hydrogen bond to E76 (Ambroggio et al., 2004; Sato et al., 2008; Tran et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Deneddylation of CRLs by CSN is rapid but can be regulated by CRL substrates.
source: Deneddylation of CRLs by CSN is rapid but can be regulated by CRL substrates (Emberley et al., 2012; Enchev et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: A CRL ubiquitination substrate bound to a substrate receptor sterically prevents concurrent binding of CSN.
source: Structural analysis suggests that a CRL ubiquitination substrate bound to a substrate receptor sterically prevents concurrent binding of CSN (Enchev et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: A CRL complex has a higher probability of being conjugated to Nedd8 as long as it is bound to substrate.
source: This suggests a model wherein a CRL complex has a higher probability of being conjugated to Nedd8 (and therefore of being shielded from Cand1) as long as it is bound to substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the steric hindrance model.

claim: Upon dissociation of substrate, a race ensues between binding of either a new substrate or CSN.
source: Upon dissociation of substrate, a race ensues between binding of either a new substrate or CSN.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the steric competition between substrate and CSN.

claim: If CSN wins the race, Nedd8 is removed, paving the way for Cand1 to initiate substrate receptor exchange.
source: If CSN wins, Nedd8 is removed, paving the way for Cand1 to initiate substrate receptor exchange.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for CRL regulation.

claim: A crystal structure of free CSN was determined by Lingaraju et al., 2014.
source: Recently, a crystal structure of free CSN was determined (Lingaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: In free CSN, Csn5 is present in an autoinhibited state wherein glutamate-104 within the 'insert-1' (INS1) sequence forms a fourth ligand to the zinc.
source: A major insight to emerge from the structure was the unexpected finding that Csn5 was present in an autoinhibited state, wherein a glutamate (Csn5-E104) within the 'insert-1' (INS1) sequence common to JAMM family members (Sato et al., 2008) forms a fourth ligand to the zinc, displacing the catalytic Csn5-E76-bound water molecule and shifting Csn5-E76.
evidence: Supported by citation to the crystal structure.

claim: Csn5-E104 binding to zinc displaces the catalytic Csn5-E76-bound water molecule and shifts Csn5-E76.
source: A major insight to emerge from the structure was the unexpected finding that Csn5 was present in an autoinhibited state, wherein a glutamate (Csn5-E104) within the 'insert-1' (INS1) sequence common to JAMM family members (Sato et al., 2008) forms a fourth ligand to the zinc, displacing the catalytic Csn5-E76-bound water molecule and shifting Csn5-E76.
evidence: Supported by citation to the crystal structure.

claim: Csn5-E104 is found in all Csn5 orthologs, but not in other JAMM proteins.
source: Csn5-E104 is found in all Csn5 orthologs, but not in other JAMM proteins, suggesting that this mode of regulation is conserved but unique to CSN.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of JAMM family members.

claim: The autoinhibitory mechanism involving Csn5-E104 is conserved but unique to CSN.
source: Csn5-E104 is found in all Csn5 orthologs, but not in other JAMM proteins, suggesting that this mode of regulation is conserved but unique to CSN.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation patterns.

claim: Binding of substrate to CSN may induce movement of the N-terminal domains (NTD) of Csn2 and Csn4 towards the cullin.
source: Comparison of the structure of free CSN to the structure of a catalytically-dead mutant CSN bound to Nedd8-conjugated SCFSkp2 determined by negative stain electron microscopy (Enchev et al., 2012) implied that binding of substrate to CSN may induce several conformational changes in the latter, including movement of the N-terminal domains (NTD) of Csn2 and Csn4 towards the cullin.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of structures.

claim: Movement of Csn2 and Csn4 NTDs might be further propagated to the Csn5/6 module.
source: The latter movement, in turn, might be further propagated to the Csn5/6 module (Lingaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis.

claim: During catalysis INS1 moves out of the active site and Csn5-E76 adopts a position similar to that observed in a crystallographic structure of Csn5 in isolation.
source: Moreover, it is reasonable to expect that during catalysis INS1 moves out of the active site and Csn5-E76 adopts a position similar to that observed in a crystallographic structure of Csn5 in isolation (Echalier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with the structure of isolated Csn5.

claim: If Csn5-E104 is mutated to an alanine, CSN more rapidly cleaves the simple model substrate ubiquitin-rhodamine.
source: Interestingly, if Csn5-E104 is mutated to an alanine, CSN more rapidly cleaves the simple model substrate ubiquitin-rhodamine (Lingaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: The primary reason for the autoinhibited state is to keep CSN off until it binds a physiologic substrate, which would prevent spurious cleavage of non-cullin Nedd8 conjugates and possibly even ubiquitin conjugates.
source: This was interpreted to mean that the primary reason for the autoinhibited state is to keep CSN off until it binds a physiologic substrate, which would prevent spurious cleavage of non-cullin Nedd8 conjugates and possibly even ubiquitin conjugates.
evidence: This is an interpretation/speculation about the functional significance of autoinhibition.

claim: Cryo electron microscopy and single particle analysis of CSN5H138A in complex with neddylated SCFSkp2/Cks1 was performed to gain detailed insights into the molecular determinants underlying activation of CSN.
source: To gain detailed insights into the molecular determinants underlying activation of CSN, we performed cryo electron microscopy (cryo EM) and single particle analysis of CSN5H138A (we use the nomenclature CSN#x where # refers to subunit number and x to the specific mutation) in complex with neddylated SCFSkp2/Cks1 (the sample is described in Enchev et al., (2012) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The Csn5-H138A mutant lacks one of the JAMM ligands that coordinate the catalytic zinc.
source: The Csn5-H138A mutant lacks one of the JAMM ligands that coordinate the catalytic zinc.
evidence: This is a description of the mutation used in the study.

claim: The Csn5-H138A mutant forms a normal CSN complex that has been extensively characterized.
source: This mutant forms a normal CSN complex that has been extensively characterized (Enchev et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: ~75000 single molecular images were used for the final three-dimensional reconstruction.
source: We used ~75000 single molecular images for the final three-dimensional reconstruction and the structure was refined to a nominal resolution of 7.2 Å, according to the 'gold standard' criterion of a Fourier shell correlation (FSC) of 0.143 (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Scheres and Chen, 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The structure was refined to a nominal resolution of 7.2 Å, according to the 'gold standard' criterion of a Fourier shell correlation (FSC) of 0.143.
source: We used ~75000 single molecular images for the final three-dimensional reconstruction and the structure was refined to a nominal resolution of 7.2 Å, according to the 'gold standard' criterion of a Fourier shell correlation (FSC) of 0.143 (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Scheres and Chen, 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a description of the resolution achieved in the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The map was low-pass filtered to 8.5 Å, according to the more stringent criterion of an FSC of 0.5.
source: To avoid over-interpretation, for the subsequent analysis we low-pass filtered the map to 8.5 Å, according to the more stringent criterion of an FSC of 0.5.
evidence: This describes the filtering applied to the cryo-EM map.

claim: There was very good match between the electron density map and the atomic coordinates for the scaffold subunits Csn1, Csn3, Csn7 and Csn8.
source: We observed very good matches between the respective map segments and the atomic coordinates for the scaffold subunits Csn1, Csn3, Csn7 and Csn8, the winged-helix domains of Csn2 and Csn4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and the helical bundle formed by the C-termini of all eight CSN subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) as well as the expected recovery of secondary structure at this resolution.
evidence: This describes the quality of fit between the model and the cryo-EM density.

claim: There was very good match between the electron density map and the winged-helix domains of Csn2 and Csn4.
source: We observed very good matches between the respective map segments and the atomic coordinates for the scaffold subunits Csn1, Csn3, Csn7 and Csn8, the winged-helix domains of Csn2 and Csn4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and the helical bundle formed by the C-termini of all eight CSN subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) as well as the expected recovery of secondary structure at this resolution.
evidence: This describes the quality of fit between the model and the cryo-EM density.

claim: There was very good overlap between the coordinates of Cul1 (with the exception of helix29 and the WHB domain) and Skp1 and the corresponding electron density segments.
source: Similarly, there was a very good overlap between the coordinates of Cul1 (with the exception of helix29 and the WHB domain, see below) and Skp1 and the corresponding electron density segments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This describes the quality of fit between the model and the cryo-EM density.

claim: The local resolution was lower without recovery of secondary structure in the N-terminal domain of Cul1.
source: However, the local resolution was lower without recovery of secondary structure in the N-terminal domain of Cul1.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The density of the substrate receptor Skp2/Cks1 was poorly defined, indicating a potential flexibility in this region.
source: Moreover, the density of the substrate receptor Skp2/Cks1 was poorly defined (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), indicating a potential flexibility in this region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM density quality.

claim: The presence of Skp1/Skp2 had modest effects on the affinity and deneddylation activity.
source: Since the presence of Skp1/Skp2 had modest effects on the affinity and deneddylation activity (see below), we did not interpret this observation further.
evidence: This is supported by binding and activity assays shown later in the manuscript.

claim: There was nearly no overlap between the EM density map and the N-terminal portions of Csn2 and Csn4, as well as the MPN-domains of Csn5 and Csn6, the RING domain of Rbx1, the WHB domain of Cul1, and Nedd8.
source: In contrast to the large segments of CSN that were unaltered upon binding substrate, there was nearly no overlap between the EM density map and the N-terminal portions of Csn2 and Csn4, as well as the MPN-domains of Csn5 and Csn6, the RING domain of Rbx1, the WHB domain of Cul1, and Nedd8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This describes the conformational changes observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A Csn2 N-terminal fragment encompassing amino acids 30 through 180 was docked as a rigid body, positioning it close to the four-helical bundle and helix 24 of Cul1.
source: A Csn2 N-terminal fragment encompassing the portion between its crystallographically resolved N-terminus (amino acid 30) through to a flexible loop at amino acid 180, was docked as a rigid body (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), positioning it close to the four-helical bundle and helix 24 of Cul1 (Zheng et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the modeling procedure used to fit Csn2-NTD into the cryo-EM density.

claim: An N-terminal fragment of Csn4, spanning amino acids 1 to 295, was docked independently as a rigid body.
source: An N-terminal fragment of Csn4, spanning amino acids 1 to 295, which ends in a previously reported hinge loop (Lingaraju et al., 2014), was also docked independently as a rigid body (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This describes the modeling procedure used to fit Csn4-NTD into the cryo-EM density.

claim: The resulting conformation of Csn4 resembles a crystal form of Csn4 observed in isolation.
source: The resulting conformation of Csn4 resembles a crystal form of Csn4 observed in isolation (Lingaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously published structure.

claim: The two N-terminal helical repeat motifs of Csn4 make contacts with the winged-helix A domain of Cul1.
source: The two N-terminal helical repeat motifs of Csn4 make contacts with the winged-helix A domain of Cul1 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, right hand panel, red arrow and green circle).
evidence: This describes an interface observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The positions of Csn2 and Csn4 delineated a density in the map which could accommodate the RING domain of Rbx1.
source: Moreover, these positions of Csn2 and Csn4 delineated a density in the map, which could accommodate the RING domain of Rbx1 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, right hand panel, black ellipse), with the RING proximal to two conserved helices between amino acids 160 and 197 of Csn4 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, black arrow) and a loop in Csn2 located between residues 289 and 306.
evidence: This describes the location of the RING domain in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The RING domain is proximal to two conserved helices between amino acids 160 and 197 of Csn4.
source: Moreover, these positions of Csn2 and Csn4 delineated a density in the map, which could accommodate the RING domain of Rbx1 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, right hand panel, black ellipse), with the RING proximal to two conserved helices between amino acids 160 and 197 of Csn4 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, black arrow) and a loop in Csn2 located between residues 289 and 306.
evidence: This describes an interface observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The RING domain is proximal to a loop in Csn2 located between residues 289 and 306.
source: Moreover, these positions of Csn2 and Csn4 delineated a density in the map, which could accommodate the RING domain of Rbx1 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, right hand panel, black ellipse), with the RING proximal to two conserved helices between amino acids 160 and 197 of Csn4 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, black arrow) and a loop in Csn2 located between residues 289 and 306.
evidence: This describes an interface observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The MPN domains of Csn5 and Csn6 were moved as rigid bodies into a neighboring map segment.
source: To improve the fit of Csn5 and Csn6, we moved their MPN domains as rigid bodies into the neighboring map segment of similar shape and dimensions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This describes the modeling procedure used to fit Csn5/6 into the cryo-EM density.

claim: After docking Csn5, two empty neighboring densities were observed which accommodated Nedd8 and the WHB domain of Cul1.
source: Importantly, after docking Csn5, we observed two empty neighboring densities (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, right hand panel, circles), which accommodated the two yet undocked protein components – Nedd8 and the WHB domain of Cul1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This describes the location of Nedd8 and WHB domain in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Helix 29 and the WHB of Cul1 (amino acids 690 to the C-terminus) were allowed to move as a rigid body towards Csn5.
source: The docking of the latter was enabled by allowing helix 29 and the WHB, amino acids 690 to the C-terminus of Cul1, to move as a rigid body towards Csn5.
evidence: This describes the modeling procedure used to fit the WHB domain into the cryo-EM density.

claim: No electron density was observed around helix 29 of Cul1, consistent with structural flexibility in this region.
source: However, we did not observe an electron density around helix 29 of Cul1, consistent with a structural flexibility in this region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the absence of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The model places the neddylated WHB domain in close binding proximity to the RING domain, as well as both INS1 and INS2 of Csn5.
source: This model places the neddylated WHB domain in close binding proximity to the RING domain, as well as both INS1 and INS2 of Csn5.
evidence: This describes the spatial relationships in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The hydrophobic patch of Nedd8 is facing INS1, and not the WHB domain, as has been reported for the isolated neddylated C-terminal domain of Cul5.
source: The hydrophobic patch of Nedd8 is facing INS1, and not the WHB domain, as has been reported for the isolated neddylated C-terminal domain of Cul5 (Duda et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes a difference between the current structure and a previously published structure.

claim: Mutagenesis of conserved charged residues in the INS2 domain of Csn5 showed reduced catalytic activity in deneddylation assays.
source: Nevertheless, to further substantiate this docking, we mutagenized conserved charged residues in the INS2 domain of Csn5 as well as the WHB domain, and as expected all of these constructs showed reduced catalytic activity in deneddylation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E, F).
evidence: This is experimental validation of the structural model.

claim: Mutagenesis of conserved charged residues in the WHB domain showed reduced catalytic activity in deneddylation assays.
source: Nevertheless, to further substantiate this docking, we mutagenized conserved charged residues in the INS2 domain of Csn5 as well as the WHB domain, and as expected all of these constructs showed reduced catalytic activity in deneddylation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E, F).
evidence: This is experimental validation of the structural model.

claim: Cross-linking coupled to mass spectrometric analysis was performed to validate the molecular docking of individual subunits and domains in the electron density map.
source: We sought orthogonal experimental validation for the molecular docking of the individual subunits and domains in the electron density map by performing cross-linking coupled to mass spectrometric analysis of the cross-linked peptides (Leitner et al., 2014) following the procedure described in Birol et al., (2014) (Supplementary files 1–6).
evidence: This describes an orthogonal validation approach.

claim: For the cross-linker disuccinimidylsuberate H12/D12, the maximum predicted distance between two cross-linked lysine residues is generally accepted to be below ~30 Å.
source: For the cross-linker used in this study (disuccinimidylsuberate H12/D12), the maximum predicted distance between two cross-linked lysine residues is generally accepted to be below ~30 Å (Politis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cross-linker used.

claim: Out of 39 high-confidence inter-subunit cross-links detected within the CSN5H138A–N8-SCFSkp2/Cks1 complex at a false discovery rate of 5 percent, the great majority was within regions of modeled atomic structure.
source: As shown in Supplementary file 1, out of the 39 high-confidence inter-subunit cross-links detected within the CSN5H138A–N8-SCFSkp2/Cks1 complex at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5 percent, the great majority was within regions of modeled atomic structure and only six links exhibited a distance larger than 30 Å when mapped onto our model.
evidence: This describes the results of the cross-linking mass spectrometry validation.

claim: Only six cross-links exhibited a distance larger than 30 Å when mapped onto the model, and all of these larger-distance links are connected to the flexibly positioned Skp2 density.
source: As shown in Supplementary file 1, out of the 39 high-confidence inter-subunit cross-links detected within the CSN5H138A–N8-SCFSkp2/Cks1 complex at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5 percent, the great majority was within regions of modeled atomic structure and only six links exhibited a distance larger than 30 Å when mapped onto our model. However, all of these larger-distance links are connected to the flexibly positioned Skp2 density.
evidence: This describes the results of the cross-linking mass spectrometry validation.

claim: Cross-linking experiments on different CSN-CRL complexes, varying the substrate receptor, the cullin and the neddylation state, were consistent with the architecture proposed for CSN5H138A-N8-SCFSkp2/Cks1.
source: Moreover, we further performed similar cross-linking experiments on a number of different CSN-CRL complexes, varying the substrate receptor, the cullin and the neddylation state (Supplementary files 2–6). All results were consistent with the architecture proposed here for CSN5H138A-N8-SCFSkp2/Cks1.
evidence: This describes additional validation of the structural model.

claim: Cross-links support proximity of K290 in Csn4 and K89 in the RING domain.
source: Intriguingly, when taking into account cross-links with an FDR of up to 0.25 (Supplementary files 2 and 3), we found two cross-links that support proximity of K290 in Csn4 and K89 in the RING domain (Supplementary file 2), as well as K32 in Csn4-NTD and K587 in Cul1, which is in the immediate vicinity of the WHA domain of Cul1 (Supplementary file 3), as suggested by our EM reconstruction.
evidence: This describes cross-linking data supporting the structural model.

claim: Cross-links support proximity of K32 in Csn4-NTD and K587 in Cul1, which is in the immediate vicinity of the WHA domain of Cul1.
source: Intriguingly, when taking into account cross-links with an FDR of up to 0.25 (Supplementary files 2 and 3), we found two cross-links that support proximity of K290 in Csn4 and K89 in the RING domain (Supplementary file 2), as well as K32 in Csn4-NTD and K587 in Cul1, which is in the immediate vicinity of the WHA domain of Cul1 (Supplementary file 3), as suggested by our EM reconstruction.
evidence: This describes cross-linking data supporting the structural model.

claim: Dansyl was conjugated to the C-terminus of Cul1 using 'sortagging' to generate dansylated Cul1/Rbx1 (Cul1d/Rbx1).
source: To this end, the environmentally-sensitive dye dansyl was conjugated to the C-terminus of Cul1 using 'sortagging' (Theile et al., 2013) to generate dansylated Cul1/Rbx1 (Cul1d/Rbx1)(Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the fluorescent substrate.

claim: Cul1d/Rbx1 exhibited normal E3 activity.
source: Cul1d/Rbx1 exhibited normal E3 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and bound CSN with an affinity similar to Cul1/Rbx1 based on their IC50 values for competitive inhibition of a deneddylation reaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Emberley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is experimental validation that the dansyl label does not interfere with function.

claim: Cul1d/Rbx1 bound CSN with an affinity similar to Cul1/Rbx1 based on their IC50 values for competitive inhibition of a deneddylation reaction.
source: Cul1d/Rbx1 exhibited normal E3 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and bound CSN with an affinity similar to Cul1/Rbx1 based on their IC50 values for competitive inhibition of a deneddylation reaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Emberley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is experimental validation that the dansyl label does not interfere with binding.

claim: When Cul1d/Rbx1 was incubated with CSN, an increase in dansyl fluorescence was observed.
source: When Cul1d/Rbx1 was incubated with CSN (all CSN preparations used in this work are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), we observed an increase in dansyl fluorescence (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental observation that forms the basis of the binding assay.

claim: The fluorescence signal was due to specific binding because it was chased upon addition of excess unlabeled Cul1/Rbx1.
source: This signal was due to specific binding because it was chased upon addition of excess unlabeled Cul1/Rbx1 (Figure 2A, titration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) or Cand1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), which competes for substrate deneddylation by CSN (Emberley et al., 2012; Enchev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is experimental validation that the fluorescence signal reports on specific binding.

claim: The fluorescence signal was chased upon addition of Cand1, which competes for substrate deneddylation by CSN.
source: This signal was due to specific binding because it was chased upon addition of excess unlabeled Cul1/Rbx1 (Figure 2A, titration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) or Cand1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), which competes for substrate deneddylation by CSN (Emberley et al., 2012; Enchev et al., 2012).
evidence: This is experimental validation that the fluorescence signal reports on specific binding.

claim: CSN bound Cul1d/Rbx1 with a Kd of 310 nM.
source: Using this assay we determined that CSN bound Cul1d/Rbx1 with a Kd of 310 nM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity from the fluorescence assay.

claim: Cul1d/Rbx1 binding to CSN was only modestly affected by the addition of free Nedd8.
source: Cul1d/Rbx1 binding to CSN was only modestly affected by the addition of free Nedd8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) or assembly with Skp2/Skp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) or Fbxw7/Skp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This describes the effect of free Nedd8 on binding affinity.

claim: Cul1d/Rbx1 binding to CSN was only modestly affected by assembly with Skp2/Skp1.
source: Cul1d/Rbx1 binding to CSN was only modestly affected by the addition of free Nedd8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) or assembly with Skp2/Skp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) or Fbxw7/Skp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This describes the effect of substrate receptor on binding affinity.

claim: Cul1d/Rbx1 binding to CSN was only modestly affected by assembly with Fbxw7/Skp1.
source: Cul1d/Rbx1 binding to CSN was only modestly affected by the addition of free Nedd8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) or assembly with Skp2/Skp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) or Fbxw7/Skp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This describes the effect of substrate receptor on binding affinity.

claim: CSN5H138A bound Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 ~200-fold more tightly than CSN bound Cul1d/Rbx1 (Kd 1.6 nM vs. 310 nM).
source: Remarkably, CSN5H138A bound Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 ~200-fold more tightly than CSN bound Cul1d/Rbx1 (Kd 1.6 nM vs. 310 nM; Figures 3A–B).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity showing the effect of neddylation and the H138A mutation.

claim: The estimated Kd for CSN5H138A binding to Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 falls well below the fixed concentration of Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 used in the assay.
source: Note that the estimated Kd falls well below the fixed concentration of Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 used in the assay. This introduces greater uncertainty into our estimate but nevertheless we can conclude with confidence that the binding of substrate to CSN5H138A is very tight (≤5 nM; see Materials and Methods for further discussion of this matter).
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the binding measurement.

claim: The binding of substrate to CSN5H138A is very tight (≤5 nM).
source: Note that the estimated Kd falls well below the fixed concentration of Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 used in the assay. This introduces greater uncertainty into our estimate but nevertheless we can conclude with confidence that the binding of substrate to CSN5H138A is very tight (≤5 nM; see Materials and Methods for further discussion of this matter).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the binding affinity based on the experimental data.

claim: Addition of Skp2/Skp1 or Fbxw7/Skp1 had comparatively minor effects on affinity of CSN5H138A for substrate.
source: As reported above for CSN binding to product, addition of Skp2/Skp1 or Fbxw7/Skp1 had comparatively minor effects on affinity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This describes the effect of substrate receptors on binding affinity.

claim: Neddylation improved affinity of Cul1d/Rbx1 for CSN5H138A by ~6-fold.
source: Thus, neddylation improved affinity of Cul1d/Rbx1 for CSN5H138A by ~6-fold, whereas the Csn5-H138A mutation improved affinity for Cul1d/Rbx1 by ~30-fold.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of binding affinities.

claim: The Csn5-H138A mutation improved affinity for Cul1d/Rbx1 by ~30-fold.
source: Thus, neddylation improved affinity of Cul1d/Rbx1 for CSN5H138A by ~6-fold, whereas the Csn5-H138A mutation improved affinity for Cul1d/Rbx1 by ~30-fold.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of binding affinities.

claim: The high affinity binding of CSN5H138A to substrate was supported by an orthogonal competition experiment in which 100 nM CSN5H138A completely blocked deneddylation of 75 nM Cul1-N8/Rbx1.
source: The high affinity binding of CSN5H138A to substrate was supported by an orthogonal competition experiment in which 100 nM CSN5H138A completely blocked deneddylation of 75 nM Cul1-N8/Rbx1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an orthogonal validation of the high affinity binding.

claim: Despite a 200-fold difference in Kd for CSN5H138A binding to substrate compared to CSN binding to product, the kon values for formation of these complexes were nearly identical (2.0 x 107 M-1 sec-1 for CSN–product and 2.2 x 107 M-1 sec-1 for CSN5H138A–substrate).
source: Remarkably, despite a 200-fold difference in Kd for CSN5H138A binding to substrate compared to CSN binding to product, the kon values for formation of these complexes were nearly identical (2.0 x 107 M-1 sec-1 for CSN–product and 2.2 x 107 M-1 sec-1 for CSN5H138A–substrate; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a measured kinetic parameter showing that kon is similar despite different Kd values.

claim: The difference in affinity between CSN5H138A binding to substrate and CSN binding to product is driven by a large difference in koff.
source: This suggested that the difference in affinity was driven by a large difference in koff.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured kon and Kd values.

claim: Substrate dissociated very slowly from CSN5E76A,5H138A, whereas product dissociated ~65-fold faster from CSN.
source: Consistent with the predictions from the Kd and kon values, substrate dissociated very slowly from CSN5E76A,5H138A, whereas product dissociated ~65-fold faster from CSN.
evidence: This is a measured koff value confirming the prediction from Kd and kon.

claim: As substrate is deneddylated to product, its affinity for CSN is strongly reduced and its koff speeds up.
source: This suggests that as substrate is deneddylated to product, its affinity for CSN is strongly reduced and its koff speeds up.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured kinetic parameters.

claim: Deletion of the first 269 amino acids of Csn2 caused a massive loss in binding to substrate (Kd > 1300 nM).
source: Deletion of the first 269 amino acids of Csn2, observed to interact with Cul1 but not the RING domain of Rbx1, caused a massive loss in binding to substrate (Kd > 1300 nM; Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity showing the importance of Csn2-NTD.

claim: The contact between Csn2-NTD and N8-SCFSkp2/Cks1 was critical to formation of the [ES] complex.
source: Thus, the contact we observed between Csn2-NTD and N8-SCFSkp2/Cks1 was critical to formation of the [ES] complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: Deletion of the first 297 amino acids NTD of Csn4 had a relatively modest effect on binding.
source: By contrast, deletion of the first 297 amino acids NTD of Csn4 (4∆N), a portion which was observed to form interfaces with both Cul1 and the RING domain of Rbx1, had a relatively modest effect; CSN4∆N,5H138A bound Cul1d/Rbx1 and Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 with Kd values of > 750 nM and 20 nM, respectively (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity showing the effect of deleting Csn4-NTD.

claim: CSN4∆N,5H138A bound Cul1d/Rbx1 and Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 with Kd values of > 750 nM and 20 nM, respectively.
source: By contrast, deletion of the first 297 amino acids NTD of Csn4 (4∆N), a portion which was observed to form interfaces with both Cul1 and the RING domain of Rbx1, had a relatively modest effect; CSN4∆N,5H138A bound Cul1d/Rbx1 and Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 with Kd values of > 750 nM and 20 nM, respectively (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity.

claim: A TEV protease cleavage site was introduced after residue 37 of Rbx1 to generate Cul1/Rbx1TEV.
source: To test the role of the RING domain in complex formation, we generated both Cul1/Rbx1 and Cul1d/Rbx1 in which the RING domain can be deleted by introducing a TEV protease cleavage site (Dougherty et al., 1989) after residue 37 of Rbx1 to generate Cul1 (or Cul1d)/Rbx1TEV (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the ΔRING substrate.

claim: After conjugating Nedd8 to the purified complex, it was treated with TEV protease to remove the RING domain, yielding Cul1-N8/Rbx1∆RING.
source: After conjugating Nedd8 to the purified complex, we treated it with TEV protease to remove the RING domain, yielding Cul1 (or Cul1d)-N8/Rbx1∆RING (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the ΔRING substrate.

claim: The truncated Cul1/Rbx1∆RING was inactive in an ubiquitylation assay.
source: The truncated Cul1/Rbx1∆RING was inactive in an ubiquitylation assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) but behaved as a monodisperse sample with the expected hydrodynamic radius upon size exclusion chromatography (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is experimental validation that the RING domain is required for E3 activity.

claim: Cul1/Rbx1∆RING behaved as a monodisperse sample with the expected hydrodynamic radius upon size exclusion chromatography.
source: The truncated Cul1/Rbx1∆RING was inactive in an ubiquitylation assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) but behaved as a monodisperse sample with the expected hydrodynamic radius upon size exclusion chromatography (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is experimental validation that the ΔRING substrate is properly folded.

claim: Cul1d-N8/Rbx1∆RING bound CSN5E76A,5H138A and CSN5E76A with affinities of 12 nM and 13 nM respectively.
source: Notably, Cul1d-N8/Rbx1∆RING bound CSN5E76A,5H138A and CSN5E76A with affinities (12 nM and 13 nM respectively; Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) similar to that observed for binding of wild type Cul1d-N8/Rbx1 to CSN4∆N,5H138A.
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity showing the effect of deleting the RING domain.

claim: The Csn4-∆N and Rbx1-∆RING mutations had largely independent effects on binding.
source: However, double mutant analysis suggested that the Csn4-∆N and Rbx1-∆RING mutations had largely independent effects on binding (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from double mutant analysis.

claim: The interaction of Csn2-NTD with neddylated substrate makes a large contribution to binding energy, with modest enhancements independently provided by the Csn4-NTD and Rbx1-RING domains.
source: The overall picture that emerged from these studies in light of the structural data is that the interaction of Csn2-NTD with neddylated substrate makes a large contribution to binding energy, with modest enhancements independently provided by the Csn4-NTD and Rbx1-RING domains.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mutagenesis and binding data.

claim: CSN5E104A bound Cul1d/Rbx1 with a Kd of 26 nM.
source: This was confirmed: CSN5E104 bound Cul1d/Rbx1 with a Kd of 26 nM (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity supporting the E-vict hypothesis.

claim: Product dissociated from CSN5H138A and CSN5E104A about eightfold more slowly than it dissociated from CSN.
source: Furthermore, measurement of koff values revealed that product dissociated from CSN5H138A and CSN5E104A about eightfold more slowly than it dissociated from CSN (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a measured koff value supporting the E-vict hypothesis.

claim: Following cleavage of the isopeptide bond and dissociation of Nedd8, INS1 of Csn5 engages the active site zinc via E104 to return CSN to its apo state.
source: We propose that dissociation of the cleaved Nedd8 also removes an impediment to Csn5-INS1, which can now bind the catalytic site zinc via E104 to return CSN to its apo state.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: Engagement of the active site zinc by Csn5-E104 accelerates the rate of dissociation of deneddylated Cul1/Rbx1.
source: This engagement, which we refer to as the 'E-vict' mechanism, is a critical step in what is likely to be a series of conformational rearrangements that include repositioning of Csn5-E76. Collectively, these movements reduce the affinity of CSN for product and accelerate its rate of dissociation by an additional order of magnitude.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: Engagement of the active site zinc by Csn5-E104 prevents CSN from becoming clogged with product.
source: This accelerates the rate of dissociation of deneddylated Cul1/Rbx1, thereby preventing CSN from becoming clogged with product.
evidence: This is a proposed functional consequence of the E-vict mechanism.

claim: Csn5-E76 also contributes to the operation of the E-vict mechanism, because CSN5E76A bound tightly to product.
source: We note that Csn5-E76 also contributes to the operation of this mechanism, because CSN5E76A bound tightly to product (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on binding data with the E76A mutant.

claim: Engagement of the active site zinc by Csn5-E104 forces Csn5-E76 into a configuration that promotes egress of product.
source: We speculate that engagement of the active site zinc by Csn5-E104 forces Csn5-E76 into a configuration that promotes egress of product.
evidence: This is speculation about the molecular mechanism.

claim: CSN2∆N has severely reduced catalytic activity.
source: We previously showed that CSN2∆N has severely reduced catalytic activity (Enchev et al., 2012), which is consistent with the binding data reported here.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: CSN4∆N exhibited a 20-fold defect in substrate cleavage.
source: CSN4∆N exhibited a 20-fold defect in substrate cleavage (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a measured kinetic parameter.

claim: The kcat for cleavage of Cul1-N8/Rbx1∆RING by CSN was reduced by ~18,000-fold relative to wild type substrate.
source: Meanwhile, the kcat for cleavage of Cul1-N8/Rbx1∆RING by CSN was reduced by a staggering ~18,000-fold relative to wild type substrate (Figures 5A–B).
evidence: This is a measured kinetic parameter showing the importance of the RING domain.

claim: The principal defect of the ∆RING substrate might be its failure either to induce the activating conformational change in CSN, and/or to position accurately the isopeptide bond in the active site.
source: Given that the neddylated ∆RING substrate bound to CSN with only modestly reduced affinity, we surmised that the principal defect of this mutant might be its failure either to induce the activating conformational change in CSN, and/or to position accurately the isopeptide bond in the active site.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of the RING domain defect.

claim: The Csn6-∆INS2 mutation slightly weakened binding to wild type product.
source: The Csn6-∆INS2 mutation slightly weakened binding to wild type product (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F) but completely suppressed the modest binding defect of the neddylated ∆RING substrate (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) and promoted an ~8-fold increase in its deneddylation rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity.

claim: The Csn6-∆INS2 mutation completely suppressed the modest binding defect of the neddylated ∆RING substrate.
source: The Csn6-∆INS2 mutation slightly weakened binding to wild type product (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F) but completely suppressed the modest binding defect of the neddylated ∆RING substrate (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) and promoted an ~8-fold increase in its deneddylation rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a measured binding affinity showing suppression of the RING deletion defect.

claim: The Csn6-∆INS2 mutation promoted an ~8-fold increase in deneddylation rate of the ∆RING substrate.
source: The Csn6-∆INS2 mutation slightly weakened binding to wild type product (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F) but completely suppressed the modest binding defect of the neddylated ∆RING substrate (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G) and promoted an ~8-fold increase in its deneddylation rate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a measured kinetic parameter showing partial suppression of the RING deletion defect.

claim: The partial suppression effected by Csn6-∆INS2 suggests that the RING domain contributes to the constellation of conformational changes in CSN that occur upon substrate binding.
source: This partial suppression effected by Csn6-∆INS2 suggests that the RING domain contributes to the constellation of conformational changes in CSN that occur upon substrate binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the suppression data.

claim: The CSN6∆INS2 enzyme exhibited a >1000-fold defect towards the Cul1-N8/Rbx1∆RING substrate, strongly indicating further functions of the RING domain.
source: Note that the CSN6∆INS2 enzyme nevertheless exhibited a >1000-fold defect towards the Cul1-N8/Rbx1∆RING substrate, strongly indicating further functions of the RING domain, which may include a potential role in substrate positioning as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic data.

claim: The RING domain may have a potential role in substrate positioning.
source: Note that the CSN6∆INS2 enzyme nevertheless exhibited a >1000-fold defect towards the Cul1-N8/Rbx1∆RING substrate, strongly indicating further functions of the RING domain, which may include a potential role in substrate positioning as well.
evidence: This is speculation about additional functions of the RING domain.

claim: Deletion of the Csn4-NTD or Rbx1-RING reduced KM in addition to reducing kcat.
source: A noteworthy feature of the deneddylation reactions carried out with CSN4∆N enzyme or ∆RING substrate is that although kcat was reduced in both cases, KM was also reduced (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic data.

claim: kcat for CSN (~1.1 sec-1) is much faster than koff measured for dissociation of substrate from the CSN5E76A, 5H138A mutant (0.017 sec-1).
source: However, kcat for CSN (~1.1 sec-1) is actually much faster than koff measured for dissociation of substrate from the CSN5E76A, 5H138A mutant (0.017 sec-1).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured kinetic parameters.

claim: Almost every binding event between CSN and substrate results in catalysis.
source: The implication of this is that almost every binding event between CSN and substrate results in catalysis, and KM (200 nM; Figure 5A and (Emberley et al., 2012) is much larger than Kd (1.6 nM, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic parameters.

claim: KM for CSN deneddylation (200 nM) is much larger than Kd (1.6 nM).
source: The implication of this is that almost every binding event between CSN and substrate results in catalysis, and KM (200 nM; Figure 5A and (Emberley et al., 2012) is much larger than Kd (1.6 nM, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured parameters.

claim: If kcat is reduced by mutation, the Briggs-Haldane equation predicts that KM should approach Kd.
source: But, if kcat is reduced by mutation, the Briggs-Haldane equation predicts that KM should approach Kd.
evidence: This is a prediction based on enzyme kinetics theory.

claim: For reactions with mutant CSN4∆N enzyme or mutant ∆RING substrate that exhibit reduced kcat, KM approaches Kd.
source: Indeed, this is exactly what we see for reactions that exhibit reduced kcat, including reactions with mutant CSN4∆N enzyme or mutant ∆RING substrate (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is experimental confirmation of the theoretical prediction.

claim: In the slowest reaction (cleavage of Cul1/Rbx1∆RING by CSN) the KM (5 nM) is in the same range as the Kd with which this substrate bound to CSN5E76A, H138A (12 nM).
source: In the slowest reaction (cleavage of Cul1/Rbx1∆RING by CSN) the KM (5 nM) is in the same range as the Kd with which this substrate bound to CSN5E76A, H138A (12 nM; Figure 3B), and approaches the Kd measured for binding of substrate to CSN5H138A (1.6 nM).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured parameters.

claim: The CSN5H138A–Cul1d/Rbx1 complex is representative of the affinity that develops during normal catalysis.
source: This provides strong support for our proposal that the CSN5H138A–Cul1d/Rbx1 complex is representative of the affinity that develops during normal catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic analysis.

claim: The kcat for CSN5E104A is 2.5-fold slower than for CSN.
source: To understand the significance of the E-vict mechansim to CSN function in vitro and in cells, we measured the kcat for CSN5E104A and observed that it is 2.5-fold slower than for CSN (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is a measured kinetic parameter.

claim: The Csn5-E104A mutation enhances the catalytic activity of CSN towards an unnatural substrate.
source: This was unexpected, because it was reported that the Csn5-E104A mutation enhances the catalytic activity of CSN towards an unnatural substrate (Lingaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: A similar reduced rate was observed for CSN5E104A in both single- and multi-turnover reactions.
source: Interestingly, a similar reduced rate was observed in both single- and multi-turnover reactions, indicating that under our specific reactions conditions, the activating conformational changes/chemical step are affected at least as much as product dissociation.
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic data.

claim: Under the specific reaction conditions used, the activating conformational changes/chemical step are affected at least as much as product dissociation for CSN5E104A.
source: Interestingly, a similar reduced rate was observed in both single- and multi-turnover reactions, indicating that under our specific reactions conditions, the activating conformational changes/chemical step are affected at least as much as product dissociation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: A partial knockout of Csn5 in HEK293T cells was generated using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: To test if Csn5-E104 contributes to CSN function in vivo, we generated a partial knockout of Csn5 in HEK293T cells using CRISPR/Cas9 (Shalem et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the cell line.

claim: The Csn5 partial knockout cell line expressed severely reduced levels of Csn5 and displayed hyper-accumulation of Nedd8-conjugated endogenous Cul1.
source: This cell line expressed severely reduced levels of Csn5 and consequently displayed hyper-accumulation of Nedd8-conjugated endogenous Cul1 (Figure 6A), but retained sufficient protein to survive.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell-based assay.

claim: Cells expressing FlagCsn5-E104A, H138A or E76A did not regain a normal pattern of Cul1 neddylation.
source: In contrast to wild type FlagCsn5, cells expressing FlagCsn5-E104A, H138A or E76A did not regain a normal pattern of Cul1 neddylation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the cell-based complementation assay.

claim: The same failure to restore normal neddylation was observed for Cul2, Cul3, Cul4A, and Cul5 in cells expressing mutant Csn5 proteins.
source: The same was observed for Cul2, Cul3, Cul4A, and Cul5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the cell-based complementation assay.

claim: Skp2 levels were reduced in cells expressing mutant Csn5 proteins.
source: Consistent with reduced CSN activity, as revealed by increased cullin neddylation, Skp2 levels were reduced in cells expressing mutant Csn5 proteins (Figure 6A)(Cope and Deshaies, 2006; Wee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an observation from the cell-based assay, consistent with reduced CSN activity.

claim: FlagCsn5–H138A retrieved high levels of Cul1-N8.

evidence: This is an observation from the immunoprecipitation experiment.

claim: FlagCsn5 carrying mutations in other core residues of the JAMM domain (e.g. H140 and D151) retrieved high levels of Cul1-N8.

claim: The FlagCsn5-E104A pull-down showed elevated levels of all cullins compared to wild type.

claim: Binding of CSN to neddylated substrate results in translocation of the N-terminal helical repeats of Csn2 towards the CTD of Cul1.
source: Binding of CSN to neddylated substrate results in a series of conformational changes in both complexes (Figure 7B). These include (i) the translocation of the N-terminal helical repeats of Csn2 towards the CTD of Cul1, (ii) the movement of the NTD of Csn4 towards the RING domain of Rbx1 and the WHA domain of Cul1, (iii) the translocation of the MPN domains of Csn5–Csn6 towards the neddylated WHB domain of Cul1, (iv) movement of the WHB domain towards Csn5, (v) the opening of the interface between Nedd8 and the WHB domain, and (vi) the formation of a new interface between Csn5 and Nedd8 probably involving the hydrophobic patch of Nedd8 and neighboring residues, as well as a tenuous interface between the WHB and the Rbx1 RING domain.
evidence: This is a description of conformational changes observed in the cryo-EM structure.
